account:
Today I have followed my appointments: the morning office visit, the mill grain inspection, lunch at home, council correspondence, and tea at the neighbour's east-bank cottage. I am now due back at the office at sixteen thirty, with an approved great-hall lighting and table inspection at eighteen hundred involving the builder. The secretary has been trying to establish the state of hall preparations but reported finding neither Freight nor the builder at their workplaces. I do not yet know whether preparations are complete. I previously saw a plank placed in the hall, but that alone does not establish today's work.

The unusual news is a repeated, vague report of a bridge or port change discussed at the bakery. Townspeople have named the baker, innkeeper, neighbour, Freight and builder as having been there in various accounts. I have not witnessed any change or learned a definite proposal, purpose, or outcome. I crossed the bridge without trouble. At tea, the neighbour explicitly said they had neither witnessed a change nor learned anything definite, so I should not treat the repeated rumour as confirmation. Reports of the baker carrying bread seem consistent with ordinary trade; I have no evidence of a connection to any crossing change. The neighbour says the baker reported a well-stocked morning market, and I saw seventy-seven hay bales available at the mill stall.

The scheduled council letters were also absent: the secretary found only my schedule copy and the updated appointment book in the office chest. I asked for the correspondence to be located by my return. This may simply be a missing or unprepared item; I have no evidence of deliberate interference. My immediate business is to return to the office, obtain any reliable updates and correspondence, and keep the evening inspection appointment.
